source.title: The Paradox of Noise: An Empirical Study of Noise-Infusion Mechanisms to Improve Generalization, Stability, and Privacy in Federated Learning

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; no truncation or garbling apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own CNN noise-infusion experiments and discusses generalization, but does not test any of the eight specified versions: it has no random-label fit, width sweep past interpolation, CNN versus fully connected comparison, optimizer or batch-size comparison, dropout intervention, magnitude-aware sharpness measure, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: Experiments compare noise infusion mechanisms and noise levels, reporting train/test accuracy and federated global accuracy/loss. These results concern noise infusion but do not directly measure any mapped version. The paper also discusses prior findings; those citations are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The study measures additive Gaussian noise effects on CNN accuracy and noise tolerance, rather than any of V1–V8. Noisy labels are Gaussian-perturbed and clipped, not fixed random labels; architecture comparisons do not isolate width beyond interpolation; dropout is present but not experimentally varied; weight noise is not a magnitude-aware sharpness measure correlated with generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion, but omits their qualification that Gaussian noise acts as implicit regularization when the model is not over-parameterized. They conclude that appropriately configured noise can improve accuracy, generalization and stability in centralized and federated CNNs, and propose SNR, PoS and PoA for assessing utility–privacy trade-offs. Their privacy claims are interpretations, rather than measured privacy guarantees.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains modified VGG-19 CNNs on CIFAR-10 with noise infusion, including centralized and federated setups; it does not reproduce the original random-label memorization experiments or the methods in the mapped versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with CNN architecture, noise-infusion mechanism, noise level, and centralized versus federated setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 6 reports one-percentage-point test-accuracy improvements with Gaussian hidden-layer noise for all three CNNs, with matching results for multiple layers and their single-layer substitutes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some Gaussian activation-noise settings modestly improve held-out accuracy in these CIFAR-10 CNNs.

fits_no_version.finding: Federated accuracy depends on architecture and noise level: Model 2 improves from 0.78 to 0.86, while Models 1 and 3 vary less; Model 3's loss rises to 1.72 at the highest noise level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Federated CNN tolerance to Gaussian activation noise varies by architecture and noise magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: Noise location affects training and test accuracy; weight noise is especially damaging to Models 1 and 3, whereas hidden-layer, gradient and label noise are generally less disruptive.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The performance effects of additive training noise depend on its location, magnitude and CNN architecture.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says the code is available in the author’s GitHub repository, but gives no URL)
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the extracted performance values. Centralized noise-level curves are presented primarily in figures, and the paper's stated accuracy and generalization claims are not tests of random-label capacity or the claim versions listed here. The Table 2 total parameter count for Model 3 is internally inconsistent with its trainable and non-trainable counts as printed.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Figure 6 and Figure 11 contain other noise-level accuracy/loss results, but the supplied flattened figure text does not reliably map all values to individual conditions; the accompanying prose reports qualitative trends and selected optima.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance random-label held-out accuracy.
Widening beyond the zero-training-error threshold with training to convergence.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under different tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Adding or removing dropout, its strength, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness correlated with generalization gaps and compared with other generalization measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. Dropout is part of the baseline architectures, not an intervention. Figure 10 transcription errors materially affect the noise-mechanism findings but do not change claim eligibility. E2 describes Table 7's three-percentage-point spread across architectures and should link to R7–R9, not R4–R6. Other noise-level results are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error across widths beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Large-batch versus small-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout intervention and its interaction with training-set size or other regularization.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
